resources.title: Formulae given in the exam
resources.summary: The formulae on Edexcel's Higher tier formulae sheet, and the ones Edexcel puts in the question itself when a question needs them. You still choose the right one and use it.
resources.statusNote: Follows the Higher tier formulae sheet for June 2025, which Pearson Edexcel calls the Exam Aid. It is printed as an insert in every paper. Ofqual, which regulates exams in England, has confirmed a formulae sheet for exams from 2028 and expects it to stay the same. Each year's sheet is published by 1 September of the year before. The cone, sphere and pyramid formulae are not on the sheet: they are printed in the question that needs them.

applications.title: Savings and loans
applications.body: £1000 saved at 3% a year for two years grows to $1000\left(1 + \dfrac{3}{100}\right)^2 = £1060.90$. A loan uses the same formula: borrow £1000 at 3% a year, pay nothing back for two years, and you owe £1060.90.

applications.title: Surveying and navigation
applications.body: A surveyor who knows two sides of a plot and the angle between them finds the third with the cosine rule, without walking across the land to measure it.

applications.title: Packaging
applications.body: A drinks can is a cylinder, a prism with a circle for its cross section, so its volume is $\pi r^2 h$. To hold 330 ml, which is 330 cm³, a can of radius 3.3 cm needs a height of $330 \div (\pi \times 3.3^2) \approx 9.6$ cm. Real cans are taller, because the top narrows and they are not filled to the brim.

items.name: Area of a trapezium
items.symbols: $a$ and $b$ the parallel sides, $h$ the perpendicular height between them

items.name: Volume of a prism
items.symbols: A cylinder is a prism, so its volume is $\pi r^2 h$

items.symbols: $r$ radius, $d$ diameter

items.symbols: $r$ the radius

items.name: Solving $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$
items.symbols: Where $a \neq 0$. The part under the root, $b^2 - 4ac$, says how many solutions there are: two if it is positive, one if it is zero, none if it is negative. Example: $2x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0$ has $a = 2$, $b = 5$, $c = -3$, so $b^2 - 4ac = 25 + 24 = 49$ and $x = \dfrac{-5 \pm 7}{4}$, which is $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$ or $x = -3$.

items.name: Pythagoras' theorem
items.symbols: Right-angled triangle. $c$ is the hypotenuse, the longest side, opposite the right angle. $a$ and $b$ are the two shorter sides.

items.name: Trigonometric ratios
items.symbols: Right-angled triangle. $c$ is the hypotenuse, $a$ is the side opposite angle $A$ and $b$ is the side next to angle $A$.

items.name: Sine rule
items.symbols: Any triangle. Side $a$ is opposite angle $A$, $b$ is opposite $B$ and $c$ is opposite $C$. Example: $A = 40^\circ$, $B = 75^\circ$ and $a = 8$ cm, so $b = \dfrac{8 \times \sin 75^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} = 12.0$ cm to 3 significant figures.

items.name: Cosine rule
items.symbols: Any triangle, with side $a$ opposite angle $A$. Example: $b = 7$ cm, $c = 5$ cm and $A = 40^\circ$, so $a^2 = 49 + 25 - 2 \times 7 \times 5 \times \cos 40^\circ = 20.38$ and $a = 4.51$ cm. To find an angle, rearrange: $\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$, which is not on the sheet. With sides $a = 7$, $b = 5$ and $c = 6$, $\cos A = \dfrac{25 + 36 - 49}{60} = 0.2$, so $A = 78.5^\circ$.

items.name: Area of a triangle
items.symbols: $C$ is the angle between sides $a$ and $b$. Example: $a = 7$ cm, $b = 5$ cm and $C = 40^\circ$ give $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 5 \times \sin 40^\circ = 11.2$ cm².

items.name: Total accrued
items.symbols: $P$ is the principal, the amount at the start. $r$ is the interest rate for each period, as a percentage. $n$ is the number of periods. The total accrued is the amount at the end.

items.name: Either
items.formula: $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$
items.symbols: $P(A)$ means the probability that $A$ happens. Example: one card from a pack of 52. $P(\text{heart or king}) = \tfrac{13}{52} + \tfrac{4}{52} - \tfrac{1}{52} = \tfrac{16}{52} = \tfrac{4}{13}$. The king of hearts is taken off once because it was counted twice.

items.name: Both
items.symbols: $P(A \text{ given } B)$ means the probability of $A$ once $B$ has happened. Example: a bag holds 5 red and 3 blue counters and two are taken out. $P(\text{both red}) = \tfrac{4}{7} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{20}{56} = \tfrac{5}{14}$.

resources.title: Formulae to learn
resources.summary: The formulae and facts you use without being given them: areas, the cuboid, arcs and sectors, straight lines, the laws of indices, compound measures, percentage change and angle facts.

applications.title: Decorating a room
applications.body: A tin of paint says how many square metres it covers. A wall 4 m by 2.5 m is $10$ m²; take away a 2 m by 0.8 m door and you are painting $8.4$ m².

applications.title: Speed cameras and journeys
applications.body: A car that covers 1.2 km in 60 seconds is doing $\dfrac{1200}{60} = 20$ m/s, which is 72 km/h: over the limit in a 30 mph zone, where 30 mph is about 48 km/h.

applications.title: Sale prices
applications.body: A coat cut from £80 to £60 has fallen by $\dfrac{20}{80} \times 100 = 25\%$. Dividing by the new price, £60, gives the wrong answer, 33%.

items.name: Triangle
items.symbols: $b$ the base, $h$ the perpendicular height

items.name: Parallelogram
items.symbols: $b$ the base, $h$ the perpendicular height, not the slanted side

items.name: Curved surface of a cylinder
items.symbols: Unrolled, it is a rectangle $2\pi r$ long and $h$ high

items.name: Arc length
items.symbols: $\theta$ the angle at the centre, in degrees, and $r$ the radius. Example: $r = 6$ cm and $\theta = 60^\circ$ give $\dfrac{60}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6 = 2\pi = 6.28$ cm.

items.name: Sector area
items.symbols: With $r = 6$ cm and $\theta = 60^\circ$: $\dfrac{60}{360} \times \pi \times 6^2 = 6\pi = 18.8$ cm².

items.name: Gradient
items.symbols: Change in $y$ over change in $x$, between two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ on the line. From $(1, 2)$ to $(4, 11)$: $m = \dfrac{11 - 2}{4 - 1} = 3$.

items.name: Equation of a line
items.symbols: $m$ the gradient, $c$ where it crosses the $y$-axis

items.name: Perpendicular lines
items.symbols: The gradients multiply to $-1$: $2$ and $-\tfrac{1}{2}$

items.name: Fractional powers
items.symbols: Root first, then power: $8^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2 = 2^2 = 4$

items.name: Density
items.symbols: 540 g in 200 cm³ is $540 \div 200 = 2.7$ g/cm³

items.name: Percentage change
items.symbols: Divide by the original amount, never the new one

items.name: Sum of the interior angles of a polygon
items.symbols: $n$ the number of sides. A hexagon: $(6 - 2) \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$, so each angle of a regular hexagon is $720^\circ \div 6 = 120^\circ$

items.name: Exterior angles of a polygon
items.symbols: So each exterior angle of a regular $n$-gon is $360^\circ \div n$

resources.title: Circle theorems
resources.summary: All eight circle theorems, each drawn and labelled, with the reason to write beside every angle in an exam answer.

blocks.body:
Every angle you find in a circle question needs its **reason** written beside it. Each theorem below has a diagram and a reason to write.

Three words to know. A **chord** is a straight line joining two points on the circle. A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at one point. A **segment** is the part of the circle cut off by a chord.

visual.alt: Circle with centre O: points A and B on the circumference with C on the major arc; angle AOB is 130° at the centre and angle ACB is 65° at the circumference, on the same arc AB

blocks.caption: **The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.** Both angles stand on the same arc. Here $130^\circ$ at the centre makes $65^\circ$ at the circumference. Reason to write: *angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference*.

visual.alt: Circle with diameter AB through the centre O and a point C on the circumference; angle ACB is a right angle and angle CAB is 35°

blocks.caption: **The angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.** An angle standing on a diameter. It is the first theorem with the centre angle at $180^\circ$. Here the angle at $A$ is $35^\circ$, so the angle at $B$ is $180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$. Reason to write: *angle in a semicircle is 90°*.

visual.alt: Circle with chords AC, BC, AD and BD forming a bow tie; angles ACB and ADB both stand on arc AB and are equal, marked x

blocks.caption: **Angles in the same segment are equal.** Angles standing on the same arc, from the same side of the chord: the bow tie. Reason to write: *angles in the same segment are equal*.

visual.alt: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with angle BAD 100° and the opposite angle BCD 80°, adding to 180°

blocks.caption: **Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$.** All four corners must be on the circle. Here $100^\circ + 80^\circ = 180^\circ$. Reason to write: *opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°*.

visual.alt: A tangent touching the circle at T, with the radius OT meeting it at a right angle

blocks.caption: **A tangent meets the radius at $90^\circ$.** At the point where the tangent touches the circle. Reason to write: *tangent and radius meet at 90°*.

visual.alt: Two tangents from an external point P touching the circle at P1 and P2, with radii to both points, right angles at the points of contact and equal tangent lengths marked

blocks.caption: **Two tangents from a point are equal in length.** From the same outside point $P$ to the two points of contact, P1 and P2. Each tangent meets its radius at $90^\circ$, so with $54^\circ$ at $P$ the angle at the centre is $360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 54^\circ = 126^\circ$. Reason to write: *tangents from a point are equal*.

visual.alt: A chord AB with the perpendicular from the centre O meeting it at its midpoint M; a right angle at M, AM and MB marked equal, and radii to A and B dashed

blocks.caption: **The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.** It cuts the chord into two equal halves, at right angles. Reason to write: *perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord*.

visual.alt: A tangent at A with chord AB; the angle between the tangent and the chord at A equals angle ACB in the alternate segment, both marked x

blocks.caption: **The alternate segment theorem.** The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. That is the angle the same chord makes at the circumference, on the other side of the chord. Here the angle between the tangent at $A$ and the chord $AB$ equals angle $ACB$. Reason to write: *alternate segment theorem*.

applications.title: Finding the centre of a circle
applications.body: A carpenter who needs the centre of a round table top draws two chords that are not parallel, and the perpendicular bisector of each. The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre, so the centre is where the two cross.

applications.title: Theatres and stadium seats
applications.body: Draw a circle through the two ends of a stage. From every seat on the same arc of that circle, the stage fills the same angle of view, because angles in the same segment are equal.

resources.title: Exact trigonometric values
resources.summary: The exact values of sin, cos and tan for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, for the non-calculator paper, and the two triangles they come from.

applications.title: Roofs and ramps
applications.body: A roof pitched at 30° rises half a metre for every metre measured up the slope, because $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}$. A slope 4 m long lifts the top of the roof by 2 m.

applications.title: Games and graphics
applications.body: Rotating a point on screen by 45° uses $\cos 45^\circ = \sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. The point $(1, 0)$ moves to $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$, which is about $(0.71, 0.71)$.

blocks.title: Exact values
blocks.note: $\tan 90^\circ$ is not defined: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, and $\cos 90^\circ = 0$. $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ is the same number as $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

blocks.body:
**Where they come from.** Cut a square with sides of $1$ along its diagonal: the two angles are $45^\circ$ and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$, so $\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

Cut an equilateral triangle with sides of $2$ down its middle: the angles are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, the short side is $1$ and the height is $\sqrt{3}$. So $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}$, $\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$.

**A pattern to check yourself.** Down the sin column the values are $\dfrac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{4}}{2}$. The cos column is the same list upside down.

**Using one.** A ladder 6 m long leans at $60^\circ$ to the ground. It reaches $6 \times \sin 60^\circ = 6 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}$ m up the wall, which is about 5.2 m.

resources.title: Graph shapes
resources.summary: The shapes of the graphs you must recognise and sketch: linear, quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential, and the sine, cosine and tangent graphs. The circle $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ is not drawn here.

blocks.body: Name a graph from its shape, and sketch one from its equation.

visual.alt: The line y equals 2x plus 1 crossing the y-axis at 1 and rising two for each one across, with the points (0, 1) and (1, 3) marked

blocks.caption: **Linear: $y = mx + c$.** A straight line. $m$ is the gradient, how far it rises for each one across, and $c$ is where it crosses the $y$-axis. Here $y = 2x + 1$.

visual.alt: The graph of y = x squared minus 6x plus 5, showing the roots at x = 1 and x = 5, the y intercept at (0, 5), and the minimum turning point at (3, -4)

blocks.caption: **Quadratic: $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.** A U shape, a parabola, symmetrical about a vertical line through its turning point. If $a$ is negative it is upside down. Here $y = x^2 - 6x + 5$. It crosses the $x$-axis at $1$ and $5$, which are its roots, crosses the $y$-axis at $5$, and turns at $(3, -4)$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals x cubed: an S-shaped curve through the origin, falling steeply to the bottom-left and rising steeply to the top-right, with five points marked, from (-2, -8) to (2, 8)

blocks.caption: **Cubic: $y = x^3$.** An S shape through the origin. It climbs steeply from the bottom left, flattens as it passes through the origin, then climbs steeply to the top right. With $-x^3$ it runs from top left to bottom right.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals 1 over x on axes from minus 4 to 4: two curved arms, one in the top-right quadrant and one in the bottom-left, each approaching both axes without touching them

blocks.caption: **Reciprocal: $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$.** Two separate curves, top right and bottom left. It never touches either axis, and there is no value at $x = 0$.

visual.alt: The exponential curve y equals 2 to the power x, passing through 0 comma 1, rising steeply to the right and approaching the x axis to the left without ever touching it

blocks.caption: **Exponential: $y = k^x$.** Crosses the $y$-axis at $1$, since $k^0 = 1$. When $k$ is more than $1$ it climbs faster and faster, and to the left it gets closer to the $x$-axis and never reaches it. When $k$ is between $0$ and $1$ it is the mirror image: it falls towards the $x$-axis on the right. Here $y = 2^x$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals sine x from 0 to 360 degrees, starting at the origin, peaking at 1 when x is 90, crossing zero at 180 and reaching minus 1 at 270

blocks.caption: **Sine: $y = \sin x$.** A wave starting at $0$, up to $1$ at $90^\circ$, back through $0$ at $180^\circ$, down to $-1$ at $270^\circ$. It repeats every $360^\circ$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals cosine x from 0 to 360 degrees, starting at 1, falling through zero at 90, reaching minus 1 at 180 and returning to 1 at 360

blocks.caption: **Cosine: $y = \cos x$.** The same wave as sine, moved $90^\circ$ to the left, so it starts at $1$. It also repeats every $360^\circ$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals tangent x from 0 to 360 degrees, drawn as separate branches with vertical gaps at 90 and 270 degrees where the curve runs off to infinity

blocks.caption: **Tangent: $y = \tan x$.** Separate branches that repeat every $180^\circ$, with gaps at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ where it is not defined. It has no largest or smallest value.

applications.title: Interest and viruses
applications.body: Money left to earn compound interest and a virus spreading unchecked both grow exponentially: each step multiplies by the same number, so the graph starts slowly and then climbs almost straight up.

applications.title: Tides and sound
applications.body: The height of the tide over a day and the air pressure in a pure musical note both follow a sine curve, or very nearly: the same up-and-down pattern repeating at a fixed interval.

applications.title: Sharing a fixed amount
applications.body: Share £120 between $x$ people and each gets $\dfrac{120}{x}$. That is a reciprocal graph: double the people and each share halves, but it never reaches zero.
